```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
library(gof)
```

The cumulative residual approach implemented by `gof` follows the
model-checking work of Lin, Wei and Ying (2002). This guide describes the
package's calculations and support boundaries. It complements the
[getting started guide](getting-started.html); it is not a substitute for
checking the assumptions of a particular analysis.

## The process and its null simulations

For residuals $e_i$ and an ordering covariate $z_i$, the cumulative process is

\[
W(t) = n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} 1\{z_i \leq t\}e_i.
\]

The selected indicators must have centered residuals under the null.
Residuals from an estimated model also depend on its fitted parameters.
The simulated process therefore combines residual multiplier sums with
an adjustment based on residual gradients and coefficient influence
contributions. Supplying residuals alone does not generally reproduce the
null distribution for an estimated model.

At selected sorted grid values $t_1,\ldots,t_m$, the implemented statistics are

\[
T_{\mathrm{Sup}} = \max_j |W(t_j)|, \qquad
T_{\mathrm{L2}} = \left\{\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}
       W(t_j)^2(t_{j+1}-t_j)\right\}^{1/2}.
\]

The L2 calculation is the norm of the left-step process on this grid.
The legacy result field `CvM` stores its p-value. A grid with one point
has zero L2 width. The `KS` field stores the Sup p-value. The data frame
method exposes the test names without requiring those historical field names.

With a positive bandwidth `b`, each cumulative indicator is replaced by
the window indicator $1\{t-b < z_i \leq t\}$. All observations at a tied
value enter together. Reducing `subset.max` changes the evaluation grid,
not the observations contributing to the sums. Full moving-window grids
include both entry events $z_i$ and exit events $z_i+b$, through the final
zero tail. A finite cap approximates this full-domain statistic. Choose
bandwidth and ordering/grid rules before inspecting responses for formal
testing; response-driven selection needs its own adjustment.

## Supported model paths

| Input | Supported interpretation and main conditions |
|:--|:--|
| `lm` and Gaussian `glm` | Independent observations or response means; precision weights allowed; positive residual degrees of freedom. |
| Binomial `glm` | Bernoulli responses or grouped/trial-weighted responses defining integer successes and failures; grouped contributions expand without refitting. |
| Poisson `glm` | Independent counts or response means with prior precision weights; fitted offsets are retained. |
| `lava::ordreg` | Converged ordinal fits on explicitly preprocessed complete data; category residuals are aggregated by the selected function. |
| `lava` Gaussian SEM | Independent subjects, complete data, valid structural covariance and invertible structural system. |
| `cumres.default` | User-supplied centered residuals, gradients and coefficient influences for independent residual units. |

Gaussian, binomial and Poisson adapters support their standard family links.
They retain the fitted coefficients and fitted rows. A converged numerical
fit is not necessarily a regular finite mean estimate. The GLM adapter checks
binomial separation and Poisson recession directions with linear programming,
and noncanonical/constrained links require numerical local interior-root
qualification. These checks reject boundary or unresolved cases before
returning p-values. They are numerical qualifications, not formally
outward-rounded interval proofs, proof of global optimality or proof that
a loose/custom fitter estimated coefficients accurately.

Weight interpretation
depends on the family: binomial weights specify trials, while normal and
Poisson weights specify response-mean precision. These interpretations are
not interchangeable with an arbitrary survey or cluster weighting scheme.

The implemented independent-unit multiplier scheme does not cover clustered,
weighted or incomplete/FIML SEM fits. These paths are rejected explicitly.
Custom residual functions and additional ordering covariates need their own
conditional-centering and influence justification; the interface cannot
deduce that justification from a numeric array.

## Structural equation models

This example fits a latent variable measured by three observed outcomes.
The diagnostic checks the residual for `y1`, ordered by a prediction of the
latent variable `eta`.

```{r sem}
set.seed(201)
sem <- lava::lvm(list(c(y1, y2, y3) ~ eta, eta ~ x))
lava::latent(sem) <- ~eta
sem_data <- lava::sim(sem, 180)
sem_fit <- lava::estimate(sem, sem_data)

set.seed(202)
sem_diagnostic <- sem_fit |>
  cumres(y1 ~ eta, full = TRUE, R = 99, plots = 6)
sem_diagnostic |> as.data.frame()
```

With `full = TRUE`, the adapter constructs a prediction using manifest
variables with no structural covariance path from the selected residual's
error. Under the Gaussian model this supplies the independence needed for
the centering argument. The selection uses structural paths, rather than
fitted coefficients happening to cancel. It is conservative when exact
path cancellations would allow additional conditioning variables.

With `full = FALSE`, observed named orderings must themselves satisfy the
structural safe-set check. A predictor that carries the selected outcome's
error is rejected, with advice to use `full = TRUE`. Explicitly forcing
exogeneity while retaining an incompatible error covariance is also rejected.

Multiple outcome/predictor requests can return a list of separately named
`cumres` diagnostics. Inspect or extract each member; it is not a single
joint test of the whole collection.

## Ordinal models

The ordinal method forms category cumulative residuals, then applies the
chosen aggregation across cumulative cutpoints. Since version 1.1.0,
`aggregate="omnibus"` is the default: it takes the Euclidean norm of the
whole cutpoint vector at each ordering value. Sup is the maximum norm;
L2 is the square root of the integral of the sum of squared components.
The same subject multipliers are used across cutpoints, preserving their
joint covariance. Continuity of this norm transfers the joint process
approximation to the combined statistics. The norm curves are nonnegative,
not zero-centered signed Gaussian curves.

This combines cutpoints for one chosen ordering. It is not an omnibus test
over all covariates or every possible model defect. Use
`aggregate="cutpoints"` (or `identity`) for signed component diagnostics.
Use `aggregate="score"` (or `sum`) for the former default, which checks the
integer-coded category-score mean only. Conditional category probabilities
can change while that score mean stays fixed, so a score-sum test can miss
important ordinal misspecification. The `aggregation` result/table field
records which interpretation applies.

```{r ordinal}
set.seed(203)
ordinal_data <- data.frame(x = rnorm(180))
latent_response <- 0.6 * ordinal_data$x + rlogis(nrow(ordinal_data))
ordinal_data$level <- ordered(cut(latent_response,
                                 breaks = c(-Inf, -0.7, 0.7, Inf)))
ordinal_data <- ordinal_data[complete.cases(ordinal_data), , drop = FALSE]
ordinal_fit <- lava::ordreg(level ~ x, data = ordinal_data,
                            family = binomial(link = "logit"))

set.seed(204)
ordinal_fit |> cumres(variable = "x", R = 99, plots = 0) |> as.data.frame()
ordinal_fit |> cumres(variable = "x", aggregate = "cutpoints", R = 99,
                      plots = 0) |> as.data.frame()
```

The supported `lava::ordreg` implementation ignores fitting arguments such
as `offset`, `subset`, `weights` and `na.action`. `gof` rejects fits that
record these options rather than diagnosing a different model from the one
the caller intended. Subset and complete the data before fitting. Adding
an offset to the diagnostic cannot supply an offset that the fitter did
not estimate. The diagnostic restores the ordinal fit's internal state
after evaluating predictions and numerical derivatives.

## Supplying residual gradients and influences

The default method is a lower-level interface for model developers. The
following unweighted linear example makes its inputs explicit:

```{r custom-interface}
set.seed(205)
custom_data <- data.frame(x = rnorm(140))
custom_data$y <- 1 + 0.4 * custom_data$x + rnorm(nrow(custom_data))
custom_fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = custom_data)
X <- model.matrix(custom_fit)
residual <- residuals(custom_fit)
gradient <- -X
influence <- (X * as.numeric(residual)) %*% solve(crossprod(X))

set.seed(206)
custom_diagnostic <- cumres(
  NULL,
  variable = cbind(x = custom_data$x),
  r = residual,
  dr = gradient,
  ic = influence,
  coef = coef(custom_fit),
  R = 99,
  plots = 0
)
custom_diagnostic |> as.data.frame()
```

Rows of `r`, `dr`, `ic` and `variable` must refer to the same independent
units. The columns of `dr` and `ic` must refer to the same fitted parameters.
Here `ic` is scaled so that $\hat\beta-\beta_0$ is approximated by
$\sum_i IC_i$. For a likelihood score, this is typically
$IC_i=I_n^{-1}s_i$, with total sample information $I_n$.
A conventional order-one influence function $\psi_i$ must be divided by
$n$ before it is supplied here. Multiplying these contributions by another
sample-size factor changes the simulation adjustment. For a different estimator, derive its
own influence representation rather than copying this OLS formula.

Residual and gradient functions can receive `coef` and additional named
arguments. A residual function may carry a `grad` attribute. If an
estimated model has no supplied gradient, numerical differentiation needs
`numDeriv`. A genuinely known mean with no estimated parameters uses
matching zero-column gradient and influence matrices; setting these
matrices to zero is not appropriate for parameters estimated from the data.

## No-information and numerically indeterminate processes

For `lm` and `glm` diagnostics, fitted score constraints can make an entire
selected process zero. For example, a two-cell model has no remaining
mean lack-of-fit information when ordered only by its fitted cells.

```{r no-information}
set.seed(207)
cells <- data.frame(group = rep(0:1, each = 40), y = rnorm(80))
cell_fit <- lm(y ~ group, data = cells)
cell_diagnostic <- cumres(cell_fit, variable = "group", R = 49, plots = 0)
cell_diagnostic$informative
cell_diagnostic |> as.data.frame()
```

When the structural detector certifies this case, `informative = FALSE`,
the curves are zero and the p-values are one by convention. That is not
evidence that the model has passed a more informative test.

A different parameterization can hide the same score constraints in
combinations of design columns. When every selected indicator is
numerically indistinguishable from score space, but exact structural
saturation is not certified, the adapter returns `informative = NA` and
withholds the p-values. It retains the computed curves for inspection.

```{r numerical-indeterminacy}
cells$x <- rep(seq_len(40), 2)
cells$hidden <- cells$x + cells$group
hidden_fit <- lm(y ~ x + hidden, data = cells)

set.seed(208)
hidden_diagnostic <- cumres(hidden_fit, variable = "group", data = cells,
                            R = 49, plots = 0)
hidden_diagnostic |> summary()
```

This check depends on the design and machine precision, not on a threshold
chosen from observed p-values or residual magnitudes. It is a sufficient
numerical diagnostic, not exact-arithmetic membership testing for arbitrary
ill-conditioned models. Ordinal intercept-only and saturated binary
score processes also have structural no-information detection: the underlying
CDF vector is set to zero before aggregation and p-values are one. For a
custom aggregator, this returns its value at the zero vector, which need
not itself be zero. Other adapters may omit the `informative` metadata;
missing metadata alone does not invalidate their returned p-values.

## What these checks do not establish

The default `cumres()` call defines a marginal residual-process check for
each ordering. The legacy native engine
pairs reused multipliers to sorted ranks separately for different orderings;
saved curve columns must not be combined as joint cross-variable draws.
The ordinal cutpoint combination is different: it uses shared subject
multipliers across its cutpoints and is valid for that joint functional.
`cumres_joint()` supplies a separate subject-coupled simulation for family
inference across prespecified orderings. Its simultaneous reference envelope
applies to the chosen family and evaluated grids; it is not a parameter
confidence interval or a test of every possible model departure.

For parameter-dependent custom orderings $x_\theta$, conditional centering
only at $\theta_0$ is insufficient. An ordering-derivative term vanishes
under the stronger condition
$E[r_{\theta_0}\partial_\theta x_\theta\mid x_{\theta_0}=t]=0$.
A sufficient construction uses fixed admissible data $Z$ for both the
ordering and its parameter derivatives, with $E[r_{\theta_0}\mid Z]=0$,
along with the required smoothness and stochastic-equicontinuity conditions.
The adapter differentiates residuals, not arbitrary ordering callbacks.
Named safe SEM predictions provide a structured construction; other
callbacks require the caller's derivation. The SEM `cumres()` endpoint checks
mean/linearity. Use `cumres_normality()` for the separate residual-ECDF
diagnostics in Sánchez, Houseman and Ryan (2009), including their nuisance
parameter-estimation correction.

This is an asymptotic Gaussian multiplier approximation. Rare events,
severe imbalance, high leverage and little effective information can make
it unreliable even with a large nominal sample and a numerically regular
fit. For example, a known Poisson mean of $10^{-12}$ with 1,000 observations
has almost no expected events; the empirical residual multiplier does not
supply exact small-count inference. No universal count cutoff or exact
finite-sample calibration is claimed for the multiplier method.
`cumres_bootstrap()` implements a separate binomial/Poisson simulation
procedure: fitted-null calibration refits every sample and remains approximate;
specified-null Monte Carlo testing requires genuinely prespecified means.
Unresolved refits are accounted for explicitly. See the
[joint, normality and bootstrap guide](joint-normality-bootstrap.html).

## Reproduce the simulation, not just the fit

Set the seed immediately before `cumres()` when reproducing an analysis.
Keep the same fitted object, data, ordering variables, grid, bandwidth,
simulation count and other diagnostic options.

```{r reproducibility}
set.seed(209)
first <- cumres(custom_fit, variable = "x", R = 99, plots = 3)
set.seed(209)
second <- cumres(custom_fit, variable = "x", R = 99, plots = 3)
identical(first, second)
```

For a fixed observed statistic, the legacy `cumres()` Monte Carlo p-value is
the fraction of simulated statistics greater than or equal to it. A
reported zero means that none of the `R` draws reached the observed
statistic; it does not establish a zero tail probability. Near an
underlying tail probability of 0.05, the binomial Monte Carlo standard
error is approximately:

```{r monte-carlo-error}
draws <- c(199L, 999L, 4999L)
data.frame(R = draws, approximate_se_at_0.05 = sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / draws))
```

Different orderings and test statistics need not be independent. Request
`cumres_joint()` explicitly when a family reference distribution is needed;
calling the legacy marginal API does not enable it automatically. The new
joint, normality and parametric-calibration endpoints use the documented
plus-one Monte Carlo convention, with minimum reported value `1/(R+1)`.
Its regression, reference and bounded simulation checks support the
implemented paths; they do not prove finite-sample calibration for every
possible fitted model or user-supplied residual function.

For an analysis archive, retain data and model provenance alongside the
diagnostic. A record can be created explicitly when saving your work:

```{r save-record, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
analysis_record <- list(
  data = custom_data,
  model = custom_fit,
  diagnostic = first,
  seed = 209L,
  rng_kind = RNGkind(),
  options = list(variable = "x", R = 99L, plots = 3L,
                 subset.max = 500L, b = 0),
  session = sessionInfo()
)
saveRDS(analysis_record, "gof-analysis.rds")
```

Exact reproduction across different R, dependency, compiler or linear
algebra versions is not guaranteed merely by recording an integer seed.
Keep those versions with the analysis so that any changes can be investigated.

## References

Lin, D. Y., Wei, L. J. and Ying, Z. (2002). Model-Checking Techniques Based
on Cumulative Residuals. *Biometrics* **58**, 1--12.
<https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341X.2002.00001.x>.

Sanchez, B. N., Houseman, E. A. and Ryan, L. M. (2009). Residual-Based
Diagnostics for Structural Equation Models. *Biometrics* **65**, 104--115.
See also the model-specific help pages for the package's support conditions.
